patient.chief_complaint: Progressive headache, left arm weakness, and a new-onset seizure
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Kenji Watanabe is a 71-year-old right-handed retired mathematics teacher who presents to the emergency department after experiencing a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home approximately two hours ago. His wife reports that over the past three weeks he has been complaining of progressively worsening right-sided headaches that are worst in the morning upon waking and occasionally awaken him from sleep. He initially attributed these to tension headaches and self-treated with over-the-counter ibuprofen with only partial relief. Over the past ten days, she has noticed increasing difficulty with his left hand — he has been dropping objects, had trouble buttoning his shirt, and his handwriting has become noticeably clumsier. She also reports subtle personality changes over the past two weeks, describing him as more irritable and less engaged in conversation than usual. Three days ago he began complaining of intermittent blurry vision, particularly in his left visual field, noting he bumped into a doorframe on his left side. This morning, while eating breakfast, his wife witnessed him suddenly stiffen, drop his fork, and fall from his chair onto the floor with rhythmic jerking of all four extremities lasting approximately 90 seconds. He was briefly unresponsive afterward and gradually became confused and drowsy. EMS was called and upon their arrival approximately 10 minutes later, he was postictal with slurred speech and marked left-sided weakness. He was transported to the emergency department where he has gradually become more alert over the past hour. He has no prior history of seizures. He denies recent head trauma, fever, neck stiffness, or weight loss, although his wife notes his appetite has been reduced over the past two weeks and he may have lost a few pounds.

mri.impression: Large heterogeneously enhancing right frontoparietal mass (5.8 x 4.3 x 4.7 cm) with central necrosis, thick irregular ring enhancement, restricted diffusion at the enhancing rim, and surrounding vasogenic edema. Significant mass effect with 8 mm leftward midline shift and effacement of the right lateral ventricle. No evidence of multifocal disease or leptomeningeal dissemination. Clinical correlation recommended.

differential_by_imaging.key_imaging_features: Large (5.8 x 4.3 x 4.7 cm) heterogeneous ring-enhancing right frontoparietal mass with central necrosis, SWI hemorrhagic foci, restricted diffusion at enhancing rim, extensive FLAIR edema, 8 mm midline shift — classic WHO grade IV glioma
No known primary cancer; CT chest/abdomen/pelvis negative; irregular infiltrative margins strongly favour primary glioma over well-demarcated metastasis at gray-white junction
Atypical demographics (71M); complete thick ring enhancement rather than open ring; marked mass effect; no MS history — glioblastoma is far more likely

differential.key_features: No known primary cancer; staging CT chest/abdomen/pelvis negative; infiltrative margins and corpus-callosum or eloquent-cortex involvement more typical of primary glioma than metastasis
In immunocompetent patients typically presents as homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass with diffuse DWI restriction and no central necrosis; ring enhancement with necrosis argues against
No fever or leukocytosis; DWI restriction at the enhancing rim (not centrally as in pyogenic pus) and elevated rCBV are inconsistent with abscess
Closed ring enhancement, marked mass effect, and central necrosis are atypical for tumefactive MS; demyelinating lesions usually show incomplete ('open') ring enhancement on the cortical side

useless_tools.rationale: Echocardiogram has no role in the diagnostic workup of suspected high-grade glioma absent a specific cardiac question (e.g., suspected paraneoplastic endocarditis)
Cardiac monitoring is unrelated to the diagnostic workup of a brain mass and adds resource cost without informing management

harmful_tools.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in suspected intracranial mass with imaging evidence of herniation: the pressure gradient created by LP risks transtentorial or tonsillar herniation. Even when LP is otherwise safe, CSF studies are low-yield for primary brain tumor diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede any lumbar puncture when a mass lesion is suspected, to identify mass effect and herniation risk before LP
Adequate pre-operative MRI characterization (mass, edema, eloquent-cortex proximity) is standard of care before neurosurgical tissue acquisition

critical_actions: Obtain urgent neurosurgical consultation for tissue diagnosis (stereotactic biopsy or maximal safe resection) and operative planning
Obtain MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol) before any invasive procedure
Administer dexamethasone (loading dose 10 mg IV, then 4 mg IV every 6 hours) to reduce vasogenic edema given imaging evidence of herniation/significant mass effect
Initiate antiepileptic therapy with levetiracetam (preferred non-enzyme-inducing AED) for documented seizure activity
Obtain pre-operative labs (CBC, BMP, coagulation, type & screen) before craniotomy/biopsy
Plan multimodal treatment per molecular and histological profile (e.g., Stupp protocol — concurrent chemoradiation with temozolomide for IDH-wildtype GBM)
Monitor blood glucose closely given anticipated corticosteroid use in a patient with diabetes; adjust antihyperglycemic regimen as needed
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform lumbar puncture with herniation risk — herniation risk
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide, alkylating chemotherapy) before tissue diagnosis is established
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given upcoming neurosurgical intervention and bleeding risk
key_reasoning_points: Combination of progressive headache (worse mornings), new focal neurological deficit, and/or new-onset seizure in an adult is a high-risk presentation requiring urgent contrast-enhanced brain MRI

MRI features of a right frontoparietal heterogeneously / ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis, perilesional FLAIR-hyperintense edema, restricted diffusion at the enhancing rim, and mass effect are characteristic of high-grade glioma
Perfusion MRI (elevated rCBV) and MR spectroscopy (elevated Cho/NAA, lipid-lactate) corroborate high-grade neoplasm and help guide biopsy targeting
Significant midline shift / herniation risk mandates urgent dexamethasone and neurosurgical evaluation; lumbar puncture is contraindicated
Definitive diagnosis requires tissue (stereotactic biopsy or surgical resection) with molecular profiling (IDH, MGMT, 1p/19q, TERT, H3K27M); imaging alone cannot substitute for histology
For IDH-wildtype GBM, current standard of care is maximal safe resection followed by the Stupp protocol (concurrent radiation + temozolomide, then adjuvant temozolomide)

Avoid ordering off-pathway advanced-imaging modalities (DaTscan, amyloid PET, FDG-PET, carotid duplex, transcranial Doppler) — they address other neurological differentials and add cost without informing glioma management
New-onset focal or generalized seizure with a focal-onset mass mandates AED therapy (levetiracetam preferred — non-enzyme-inducing, fewer interactions with temozolomide)

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward - classic presentation with progressive headache, left arm weakness, new-onset seizure, and a large right frontoparietal mass with midline shift on imaging
clinical_pearls: Glioblastoma is the most common and most aggressive primary brain tumor in adults, with median survival of 14-16 months with standard treatment
The Stupp protocol (surgical resection followed by 6 weeks concurrent temozolomide/radiation then 6 cycles adjuvant temozolomide) remains the standard of care
MGMT promoter methylation is present in approximately 40-45% of glioblastomas and is associated with improved survival with temozolomide therapy
New-onset seizure in an adult over 40 should always raise suspicion for a brain tumor until proven otherwise
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 4 required tools, no embedded red herrings; classic GBM presentation with clear imaging pattern (ring-enhancing mass with necrosis, edema, mass effect) and unambiguous molecular features on biopsy
